# Part 5: Knowledge Architecture

## 5.1 The knowledge estate

An enterprise does not have a corpus. It has a **knowledge estate**: everything the organization knows, distributed across systems nobody inventoried, in states nobody recorded, owned by people who have mostly left. Retrieval is a read operation against this estate. Every property of the estate becomes a property of the answer, which is why a retrieval project that begins with an embedding model has already skipped the only work that determines whether it succeeds.

**The estate has three physical forms and the distinction governs what you can do about each.**

| Form | Where it lives | Retrievable today | The intervention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Explicit** | Documents, wikis, tickets, policies, code comments, recorded decisions | Yes, subject to access and quality | Document engineering, indexing, governance |
| **Tacit** | In people's heads. Judgment, precedent, the reason the exception exists, who to call | No | **Elicitation.** Interview, shadow, write it down. This is a content project, not an engineering project |
| **Embedded** | Encoded in system behavior: validation rules, workflow branches, spreadsheet formulas, database constraints | No, and it is frequently the authoritative version | **Extraction into a tool call or a written rule.** Retrieval over a description of the rule is not the rule |

The third row is the one architects get wrong. When a business rule lives in a configuration table in the enterprise resource planning system, the wiki page describing it is a **stale copy** by construction. Retrieving the wiki page returns a confident, well-formatted, out-of-date answer. The correct design routes that question to the system, not the index. That is the retrieval-versus-tool-call boundary applied to the estate rather than to a single query.

**Decision rule:** if the knowledge is embedded in a system that can be queried, call the system; if it is tacit, commission the writing before commissioning the pipeline; only explicit knowledge is a retrieval problem.

### The inventory method

The inventory is a register with **eight columns**, and it is built by walking the questions users actually ask, not by walking the file shares. Walking the file shares produces a catalog of everything and a map of nothing.

| Column | What it records | Why it is load-bearing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Knowledge domain** | The question class, phrased as users phrase it | Domains, not repositories, are the unit of coverage |
| **Location** | System, path, format | Determines ingestion cost and parse risk |
| **Owner** | A named human with the authority to change it | An unowned document cannot be corrected, so it cannot be trusted |
| **Authority** | Authoritative, derived or copy | The single most valuable column, and almost never present |
| **State** | Current, aging, stale, contradicted, unknown | Drives triage |
| **Effective dates** | In force from, in force until, superseded by | Makes time-boundedness machine-readable |
| **Sensitivity** | Classification and access population | Sets the population a retrieved chunk may be exposed to, and so the filtering the pipeline must enforce before ranking. Only at the most restricted classifications does it decide whether the content may be copied into an index at all |
| **Query traffic** | Observed or estimated volume of questions it answers | Ranks the whole backlog |

**The authority column is the finding, not the field.** Running it across a real estate produces the same result everywhere: several documents claim to be authoritative on the same topic, none of them says so explicitly, and the one users trust is neither the newest nor the one legal approved. Writing the column forces someone to decide, and the decision is worth more than the pipeline.

**Decision rule:** every knowledge domain gets exactly one authoritative source and every other artifact in that domain is labeled derived or copy, or the domain is not ready for retrieval.

### The three enterprise knowledge failures

**Only one of these three is a retrieval problem, and it is the least common.**

| Failure | Symptom | What it actually is | The fix | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **It does not exist in writing** | The assistant hedges, generalizes or invents. Subject matter experts say "that's not how we do it" | A content gap. Tacit knowledge never elicited | Write it. Interviews, decision capture, playbook authoring | The business function |
| **It exists in twelve conflicting versions** | The assistant answers differently on re-ask. Two users get two answers. Both citations are real | A governance gap. No authority designation, no supersession | Designate, deprecate, tombstone. Reduce twelve to one | Knowledge governance |
| **It exists and nobody can find it** | The right document is in the corpus and does not come back, or comes back below the cut | A retrieval problem | Chunking, indexing, metadata, reranking | Engineering |

An architect who cannot tell these apart will spend a quarter tuning retrieval against a corpus that contains two contradictory policies and no answer to the third most common question. **The diagnostic is cheap: take the top fifty real queries, hand-search the corpus, and record for each whether a correct answer exists, exists more than once or is simply absent.** That single exercise, done before any pipeline work, reallocates the program.

**Decision rule:** classify every observed failure as absence, contradiction or invisibility before proposing a fix, because the three fixes have different owners and only the third belongs to engineering.

### Worked example: a mid-size insurer's claims knowledge estate

A claims organization commissions an assistant for first-line claims handlers. The inventory covers eleven knowledge domains. Results:

- **Four domains are authoritative and current.** Policy wordings, regulatory notification timelines, the fraud referral criteria and the reserving standard. These are ready.
- **Three domains are contradiction failures.** Escalation thresholds appear in the claims manual, in a team wiki and in a training deck, with three different monetary limits, all real, none dated. Users had been asking the team leader. The assistant would have picked one at random.
- **Two domains are absence failures.** How to handle a claim where the policyholder is deceased and the estate has not been appointed, and what to do when a supplier invoice exceeds the approved estimate. Both are pure tacit knowledge held by two long-serving handlers.
- **Two domains are embedded.** Coverage limits and excess amounts live in the policy administration system. Any document stating them is a snapshot.

The delivered design indexes four domains, routes two to a tool call, opens a content workstream for two and a governance workstream for three. **Retrieval scope was cut from eleven domains to four and the assistant was materially more useful than a version indexing all eleven**, because the four it covered it covered correctly and it declined the rest rather than guessing.

## 5.2 Document engineering

**Document engineering** is writing documents so a machine can use a fragment of them without the rest. It is a writing discipline, not a pre-processing step, and it is the highest-leverage unglamorous work in the whole field.

**The boundary of this section, stated once.** Everything below assumes a source from which text and structure can be extracted: a document, a record, a page with markup or layout a parser can read. Scanned images, photographs, audio and video belong to the same estate and enter it by a different path, whose first stage is extraction rather than parsing. The consequence is that **extraction quality becomes a measured input rather than an assumption**, carrying a confidence figure, a sampling method and an owner in the way any other source property does. The classification, retention and evidence questions these formats raise are not new questions. They are the same questions asked of an input whose text is a reconstruction of lower confidence rather than the thing itself.

### The seven properties of a machine-usable document

| Property | Requirement | Failure it prevents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chunk-aware structure** | Sections sized to be retrievable units. One idea, one section | A chunk containing half of two ideas |
| **Self-containment** | Each section names its own subject, scope and conditions | The retrieved chunk that says "this also applies to them" |
| **Explicit headings** | Headings that state the content, not the sequence. "Approval thresholds for supplier payments" not "Section 4.2" | Headings that carry no retrieval signal |
| **Resolved reference** | No unresolved pronouns, no "as noted above", no "the preceding section" | Reference that breaks the moment the chunk is separated |
| **Table over prose for structured facts** | Thresholds, limits, mappings and eligibility as tables with headers | Numbers buried in narrative and retrieved without their qualifier |
| **Front matter** | Owner, effective date, review date, jurisdiction, status, supersedes | Time-blind and permission-blind retrieval |
| **Explicit supersession** | Superseded documents say what replaced them and when | The old policy answering as though it were current |

**The orphan chunk test** is the single mechanical check that catches most of this. Take any section, cut it out of the document, hand it to a competent colleague with no other context and ask three questions: what is this about, when does it apply and does it still apply. If any answer requires the rest of the document, the section is an orphan and will be retrieved as one.

**Decision rule:** a section that fails the orphan chunk test is rewritten or excluded from the index, because a chunk that cannot stand alone in a reviewer's hands will not stand alone in a context window.

### Before and after

Badly engineered, and entirely typical of a real policy corpus:

```
4.2  Thresholds

As noted above, the same limits apply to them, save where
the exception in the preceding paragraph is engaged. Following
last year's review, the figure was increased. Where the amount
exceeds the limit, approval should be sought from the
appropriate authority before the payment is released. Regional
variations may apply.
```

Retrieved alone, this chunk states no subject, no number, no date, no approver and no jurisdiction. It is fluent, it is real and it is worse than nothing, because a model will use it and a citation will point at it.

Well engineered:

```
---
title: Approval thresholds for outbound supplier payments
owner: Head of Procurement Operations
status: authoritative
effective_from: 2026-01-01
review_due: 2027-01-01
supersedes: Procurement Policy s.4.2 (in force 2023-06-01 to
  2025-12-31)
jurisdictions: [UK, IE, DE]
audience: [procurement, accounts-payable]
---

Approval thresholds for outbound supplier payments

This section states the approval required before an outbound
payment to a supplier is released. It applies to procurement
and accounts payable staff in the UK, Ireland and Germany from
1 January 2026. It does not apply to intercompany transfers,
which are covered in "Intercompany settlement approvals".

| Payment value (EUR) | Approver              | Evidence required     |
| ------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- |
| Up to 10,000        | Line manager          | Purchase order        |
| 10,001 to 100,000   | Finance business ptnr | PO and contract ref   |
| Above 100,000       | Chief Financial Ofcr  | PO, contract, sign-off|

Exception: emergency payments to restore a safety-critical
service may be released by the on-call duty director at any
value, with retrospective approval recorded within two working
days. See "Emergency payment procedure".
```

Every property is present. The chunk names its subject, its population, its dates, its exclusions and its exception, and the numbers sit in a table with their qualifiers attached. Where the first document's heading was a sequence number, this one's heading line states the content. **This version answers correctly when retrieved alone; the first version cannot answer correctly under any retrieval configuration.** No amount of chunking strategy repairs the first one, which is the point.

### The retrofit problem

You cannot rewrite the corpus. A large enterprise policy estate runs to tens of thousands of documents and the authors are busy. So the question is never "how do we fix the corpus", it is "which two hundred documents do we fix first".

**Triage on two axes: query traffic and stakes.**

```
             HIGH STAKES
                  |
   REWRITE NOW    |   REWRITE NOW
   (rare, costly  |   (the core 200:
    errors: legal,|    high traffic,
    safety, reg)  |    high consequence)
                  |
 LOW  ------------+------------  HIGH  TRAFFIC
                  |
   LEAVE          |   METADATA ONLY
   (archive or    |   (front matter +
    exclude from  |    headings; full
    the index)    |    rewrite later)
                  |
             LOW STAKES
```

Four quadrants and three treatments, with two of the quadrants getting the rewrite, separated by priority rather than by method:

| Quadrant | Treatment | Effort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High traffic, high stakes** | Full document engineering. Rewrite, front matter, tables, orphan test on every section | Days per document. This is the funded workstream |
| **Low traffic, high stakes** | Full engineering, but ordered behind the core set. Frequently the regulatory obligations nobody asks about until they do | Days per document |
| **High traffic, low stakes** | **Metadata retrofit only.** Add front matter, fix headings, resolve the worst references. Leave the prose | Under an hour per document, scriptable in part |
| **Low traffic, low stakes** | **Exclude from the index.** Not deleted, not retrievable | Minutes. The cheapest quality improvement available |

**Excluding is an improvement.** A corpus is a population and precision falls as you add material that never answers anything. The instinct to index everything because storage is cheap misprices the cost, which is not storage, it is the dilution of every retrieval.

**Decision rule:** rank documents by observed query traffic times consequence of error, fully engineer the top two hundred, metadata-retrofit the next thousand and exclude the tail from the index.

## 5.3 Chunking and indexing

Retrieval pipeline design is three named sub-decisions: how a corpus is broken into chunks, how the chunks are indexed and how the retrieval strategy is matched to the query patterns the system will see. The first two are chosen from two different facts about the same system, and that difference organizes this section. **Chunking is chosen by what the corpus is. Indexing is chosen by how queries are phrased.** This section is the design method; the same system in operation, with owners and instruments attached, is the thirteen-stage pipeline of 5.4.

### Chunking: chosen by what the corpus is

**A chunk is the unit that gets retrieved.** The definition is worth having exactly, because it makes chunking a retrieval decision rather than a pre-processing decision. And **the chunking approach is chosen by the structure of the source material, not by a default size**, which rules out the most common wrong move in the topic: picking a token count first and structuring around it.

| Approach | How it works | When it earns its place | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Fixed-size** (with overlap) | Split into uniform spans with overlap, regardless of structure | Homogeneous, unstructured text where natural boundaries are weak; simplest to operate | The blind blade cuts mid-thought and the overlap duplicates content |
| **Semantic** | Split on meaning boundaries, topic shifts, sentence groups that hang together | Prose where a retrieved chunk must be self-contained to answer well; reduces mid-idea cuts | Hardest to build, most expensive to run |
| **Hierarchical**, also called structure-based | Preserve document structure, sections and subsections, and retrieve at the level that fits | Structured documents (contracts, manuals, policies) where section context carries meaning | Fails where documents lack reliable structure |

Read the third column as the answer key it is: each row is a scenario-to-approach mapping.

- **Homogeneous, unstructured text with weak natural boundaries takes fixed-size**, and the tiebreak is in the row: simplest to operate. When two approaches would work, operational simplicity decides.
- **Prose where a retrieved chunk must be self-contained takes semantic.** The stated benefit is that it reduces mid-idea cuts, which is the specific defect fixed-size chunking produces in prose.
- **Structured documents where section context carries meaning take hierarchical.** Contracts, manuals and policies are the standing examples, and for a legal or governance corpus this is the row that comes up in practice.

**The phrase "section context carries meaning" is the discriminator between hierarchical and semantic**, and it is worth being able to state. In a contract, a clause means what it means partly because of the article it sits under. A semantic chunker that cuts on meaning boundaries can produce a chunk that reads coherently and has lost the section that governs it. Hierarchical chunking keeps the structure precisely because the structure is part of the content. Note that hierarchical chunking is wider than cutting along structure: it also retrieves at the level that fits, which is a retrieval-time choice as well as an indexing-time one.

**The discriminator between fixed-size and semantic is self-containment, not text quality.** The two compete over the same material, prose without strong structure, so the tiebreak has to come from their own selectors. Fixed-size carries operational simplicity. Semantic carries the requirement that a retrieved chunk stand alone. **The question to ask is whether one chunk has to carry the whole answer.** If the answer can be assembled from two or three adjacent retrieved spans, fixed-size is enough and its operational simplicity decides. If a single chunk has to stand alone, semantic earns its cost.

Whatever the approach, **experiment with chunk size, boundary and overlap** rather than adopting a default, which is Anthropic's stated implementation advice. Small chunks retrieve precisely and lose context; large chunks carry context, dilute the match and consume more window per hit.

### Indexing: chosen by how queries are phrased

**Indexing decides what "similar" means when a query arrives. The strategy is chosen by the query pattern.** That first sentence is the definition to keep. Indexing is not storage. It is the operative definition of similarity, chosen in advance, applied to every query that arrives.

| Strategy | What it matches | When it earns its place |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dense** (embeddings) | Semantic similarity, meaning, not words | Queries phrased differently from the source; paraphrase, intent, concept matching |
| **Sparse** (keyword, e.g. BM25) | Exact terms, identifiers, codes, names | Queries that hinge on specific tokens: part numbers, statute citations, error codes |
| **Hybrid** | Both, with the results combined | Mixed query patterns, the common production case; recovers the exact-match results dense retrieval misses |

Dense retrieval is also called semantic search, and sparse retrieval lexical search; the distinction is the same one under either vocabulary. Dense handles paraphrase, synonyms and concepts, and is weak on exact strings: product codes, case numbers, acronyms, defined terms. Sparse matches words, weighting rare ones more heavily, so it nails exact terms and has no idea attorney and lawyer are the same idea. Neither suffices alone, which is why production systems run both and merge.

Three things in the table are load-bearing.

1. **Statute citations are a standing example of a sparse-retrieval query**, alongside part numbers and error codes. For a legal corpus this row is the whole answer: citations are exact tokens, dense retrieval will miss them and a purely semantic index over a body of law is a design error.
2. **Hybrid is the common production case.** Not the sophisticated option, not the expensive option: the common one. A design that treats hybrid as an optimization to be justified has the emphasis wrong; it is the default for mixed query patterns.
3. **The hybrid row states its direction of benefit precisely: it recovers the exact-match results dense retrieval misses.** Hybrid is dense plus a recovery of what dense loses, not a neutral blend. The measured results later in this section say the same thing in numbers: adding contextual BM25 alongside contextual embeddings removes roughly a fifth of the failures that survive the embeddings step, and it is the step most implementations skip.

#### Reciprocal rank fusion

When a hybrid index returns two ranked lists, they must be merged into one. **Reciprocal rank fusion** is the standard, low-tuning way to do it: each result is scored by its rank in each list, and the combined score favors items that rank well in both. Three properties matter.

- **Standard.** It is the expected answer, not one option among several.
- **Low-tuning.** This is the reason it is the default: it needs no weight calibration between the two lists, which is the part that otherwise becomes a maintenance burden.
- **Scored by rank in each list, favoring items that rank well in both.** Rank, not score. That is what makes it low-tuning: it never has to reconcile two incompatible scoring scales.

Why rank beats score, stated once because designs turn on it. A dense index returns cosine similarities on one scale and a sparse index returns BM25 scores on another, and the two have no common unit. Any fusion that adds or weights the raw scores has to invent a conversion, and that conversion is a tuning parameter someone has to own as both indexes change. Discarding the scores and keeping only the ordinal position removes the parameter. **Reject any proposal to tune a blend weight between the two lists**, because the whole point of the named default is that there is no weight to tune.

The architect-facing point: combining dense and sparse results is **a design decision with a known, defensible default**. The recurring move is the one to internalize: name the decision, then supply the default, so the decision does not become a research project.

### The two decisions are independent and the grid is three by three

**Chunking and indexing are chosen from two different facts about the same system, and neither one determines the other.** The selectors say so themselves: chunking follows **the structure of the source material**, indexing follows **the query pattern**. Different inputs, different decisions.

That matters because the two tables sit next to each other and both have three rows, which invites reading them as a pairing, fixed-size with dense, semantic with sparse, hierarchical with hybrid. **There is no such pairing and none of those three pairs is even a common one.** All nine combinations are legal. Hybrid is the common production case for every chunking approach, not the partner of one of them.

The worked case makes it concrete. A contract corpus queried by clause citation takes **hierarchical** chunking, because section context carries meaning, and **sparse or hybrid** indexing, because citations are exact tokens. Two answers from two facts. Change how the corpus is written and the chunking answer moves. Change how users phrase questions and the indexing answer moves. Neither change touches the other.

This is also the cleanest discriminator for a design review. A real scenario supplies both facts, one about what the documents are and one about what users ask, and each governs one decision. **A design that justifies a chunking choice by citing query phrasing, or an indexing choice by citing document structure, has the selector wrong.** It will read as reasonable and it will be defending the right answer with the wrong reason, or the wrong answer with a reason that sounds like the right one. Check the selector before you check the choice.

### Articulating the trade-off

Every retrieval design makes trade-offs among three things, each with its question attached:

| The three | The question |
| --- | --- |
| **Retrieval quality** | Does the right chunk come back? |
| **Latency** | How long does retrieval add to each request? |
| **Maintenance** | How much does the pipeline cost to keep correct as the corpus grows and changes? |

The questions are the discriminators, so learn the three with their questions attached. Does the right chunk come back is not answerable from the output, which is the risk paragraph's whole point below. How long does retrieval add to each request is per-request, not per-session. And the maintenance question is the only one of the three with time in it, and it is the one that gets forgotten, because a pipeline is priced at build and paid for continuously.

The two directions of movement:

| Move | Quality | Latency | Maintenance | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Smaller chunks + hybrid indexing** | Up | Up (worse) | Up (worse) | Up |
| **Larger chunks + dense-only indexing** | Down on exact-match queries | Down (better) | Down (better) | Down |

**Quality and latency move together in the same direction, and that is the sentence to remember.** The instinct is to treat quality and latency as opposed, one bought with the other. Here they are not opposed; they are correlated, because the same two moves that raise quality also raise latency. The trade-off is not quality against latency. It is **quality against latency, maintenance and cost jointly**. And the named loss on the cheap side is specific: larger chunks and dense-only indexing do not degrade gracefully across the board, they **miss exact-match queries**, the particular class the sparse row exists for. That connects the trade-off directly back to the indexing table, and it is why the two tables have to be read together.

The deliverable here is articulating the trade-off, not choosing an optimum. **There is no universally right point, only the point that fits this corpus and these queries, stated as a trade-off you can defend.** An architect is a person who can say what a choice costs. Three proposal shapes fail that test in review, and all three read well: a design that raises retrieval quality without naming what it costs, a design that frames the choice as quality against latency and a design that claims to have found the universally right point.

### Cost, complexity and risk

**Cost.** Hybrid indexing and smaller chunks raise both retrieval compute and per-request latency. **Size the pipeline to the query patterns you actually have, not to the most thorough one imaginable.** That names the failure mode precisely: designing for hypothetical queries. The evidence you need is the query log, not the imagination.

**Complexity.** Every chunking and indexing choice is something to maintain as the corpus changes. **A pipeline that was correct at launch can degrade silently as documents are added.** This silent failure has a time dimension the others lack. The system is not wrong when built. It becomes wrong. Nothing changes in the code, which makes it invisible to every kind of testing that runs at build time, and that is the argument for a labeled retrieval set that runs continuously.

**Risk.** ⧉ **The failure mode is a confident answer built on the wrong chunk, and retrieval quality is not visible in the output: it has to be measured against a labeled set, which is why this work ties straight to evaluation (8.2).** Three claims, each load-bearing. First, retrieval quality is not visible in the output: you cannot tell a good retrieval from a bad one by reading the answer, which is the mechanical reason retrieval failures present as model failures. Second, it has to be measured against a labeled set, meaning known queries with known correct chunks. Not sampled, not reviewed, not inferred from user complaints. **The instrument is named in 8.6, as a labeled retrieval set run daily or continuously against corpus drift and index staleness**; 8.2 governs how the set is built and graded. Third, this work ties straight to evaluation: a retrieval design is not complete until it names the evaluation instrument that will see its failures.

### The threshold question

Before designing a pipeline, ask whether you need one. Anthropic's guidance is specific: **for knowledge bases under roughly 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages, the better option is often to include the entire knowledge base in the prompt and skip retrieval entirely**, using prompt caching to make it economical.

This is the highest-value single fact in the section, because it is a named number attached to a real decision and the correct answer is the counter-intuitive one. A retrieval pipeline is infrastructure you maintain forever: ingestion, indexing, freshness monitoring, permission filtering. Skipping it when the corpus fits wins on accuracy, latency, cost and maintainability simultaneously.

### The seven design stages

For a corpus that clears the threshold, the design sequence has seven stages.

**1. Ingest**, with metadata. Metadata is frequently the highest-leverage part of the pipeline, because filtering by type, date, jurisdiction, owner or tenant before searching eliminates whole classes of wrong answer. Worth checking **before** reaching for anything more sophisticated: a solid chunk schema with titles, section names, repository paths, service names and version tags may recover enough context on its own.

**2. Chunk**, by the structure of the source material, using the chunking table above.

**3. Embed and index.** Convert each chunk to a numeric representation of meaning. Anthropic reports finding Gemini and Voyage embeddings effective, and the embedding model is a variable worth testing.

**4. Retrieve**, with both methods, dense and sparse, merged by reciprocal rank fusion as above. Neither method suffices alone; production systems run both.

**5. Rerank.** The documented procedure is specific and worth knowing as a shape: **retrieve a wide initial candidate set, in Anthropic's tests the top 150; pass those plus the query through a reranking model; select the top-K, in their tests 20; pass those into the prompt.** Reranking provides better responses **and reduces cost and latency**, because the model processes less information. The latency cost of the rerank call itself is on the order of a hundred to a few hundred milliseconds.

**6. Assemble and generate.** Question plus retrieved chunks with sources attached, and an instruction to answer from the supplied material and to say when it does not contain the answer.

**7. Cite.** Require each claim to carry its source. The platform has a **citations** feature for this, which is worth knowing exists rather than treating citation as purely a prompting problem.

### Contextual retrieval

The problem: a chunk pulled from its document loses its bearings. "The department exceeded these targets" means nothing alone and retrieves badly.

The technique: before embedding, have a model write a brief situating note for each chunk and prepend it. Anthropic's own contextualizer prompt supplies the whole document plus the chunk and asks for short succinct context to situate the chunk within the overall document for the purpose of improving search retrieval, answering with the context and nothing else.

**The measured results, on top-20 retrieval failure rate:**

| Configuration | Failure rate | Reduction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Traditional retrieval-augmented generation | 5.7% | baseline |
| Contextual embeddings | 3.7% | **35%** |
| Contextual embeddings **plus** contextual BM25 | 2.9% | **49%** |
| Plus **reranking** | 1.9% | **67%** |

Two things to take from the table. First, **the largest single reduction comes from contextual embeddings on their own**, 5.7 to 3.7, worth two points; contextual BM25 then takes off a further 0.8 and reranking a further 1.0, which makes the lexical step the smallest of the three increments and also the one people skip. Second, these stack, which is why Anthropic's recommendation is to combine contextual embeddings with contextual BM25 plus reranking and pass twenty chunks.

Practical notes from the same source: keep the generated context short, on the order of 50 to 100 tokens, since long context defeats the purpose of small chunks; use a cheap fast model to generate it; and **cache the full document while generating context for its many chunks**, which is where prompt caching turns a prohibitive pre-processing cost into a trivial one.

### Design-time failure diagnosis

Diagnosis is the skill the stage list exists to serve, so learn the symptom-to-cause map rather than the assembly order. Each symptom below points at a missing or mischosen design element:

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Exact identifiers never found | Purely semantic search with no lexical component |
| Conceptual questions answered poorly | Purely lexical search with no semantic component |
| Plausible but off-topic content retrieved | Chunks too large, missing metadata filters or near-duplicates in the corpus |
| Chunks retrieve poorly and read as anonymous even with full metadata | The case contextual retrieval is for |
| Answers cite content the user may not see | Retrieval not filtered by permission or tenant before similarity |
| Quality decays as the corpus grows | No filtering strategy; the index doing work metadata should do |
| Answers stale despite fresh source data | Ingestion not running, or index not updated |

Failures observed in operation are localized with the thirteen-stage diagnostic table in 5.4, which also carries the boundary test between retrieval failures and generation failures.

### Matching strategy to data shape and query pattern

The chunking and indexing selectors generalize into a fuller mapping. By data shape:

| Shape | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Long prose with reliable structure: contracts, statutes, manuals | Hierarchical chunking on natural units; hybrid search; metadata filters on type and date |
| Short self-contained records: FAQs, product entries, ticket summaries | One chunk per record, no splitting; lexical weighted heavily, since users search by name and identifier |
| Tables and numbers | **Do not retrieve.** Query the source system, or use code execution to compute over it. Retrieved table fragments produce confident arithmetic errors |
| Code | Hierarchical chunking by function or file, plus symbol search. Anthropic notes code retrieval punishes vague chunks hard, because near-duplicate snippets are everywhere and queries rarely share the snippet's wording |
| Heterogeneous corpus, many types and owners | Metadata filter first, then search the filtered set |
| Frequently changing corpus | Incremental reindexing with version tracking, plus a check that index and source agree |
| **Corpus under roughly 200,000 tokens** | **Skip retrieval.** Put it in the prompt and cache it |
| Highly sensitive or multi-tenant | Permission and tenant filters **before** similarity |

By query pattern:

| Pattern | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Known-item lookup: "show me contract 4471" | Lexical or direct identifier lookup. Semantic search is the wrong tool |
| Conceptual or paraphrased | Semantic search plus reranking |
| Multi-hop: "which vendors are affected by the rule that changed in March" | Decompose the query, or retrieve iteratively, feeding each answer into the next search |
| **Aggregate or counting: "how many contracts include this clause"** | **Retrieval cannot answer this.** Retrieval samples; it does not enumerate. Use a structured query, or extract into a database first |
| Comparative across documents | Retrieve per document with metadata separation, then compare in a second pass |
| Recency-sensitive | Date filter or recency weighting, and require dates in output so two measurements from different periods are not misread as a contradiction |
| Open-ended exploration | Progressive: surface a catalog first, then let follow-ups drive retrieval |

The counting row is the one people get wrong in practice. A retrieval system asked how many documents contain something answers confidently from the handful it retrieved. That is a design error, not a model error.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question the pipeline design does not ask.** The index is a governed copy of regulated records with the source system's access rules stripped off. Who owns what is in the corpus, and do entitlements survive the copy.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Selecting and ingesting a corpus | Classification, retention, legal hold and erasure applied to chunks and embeddings | Retention schedule extended to derived artifacts. Records manager with the data owner |
| Designing retrieval | Entitlement and tenant filtering inherited from source and applied before similarity | Entitlement design with test evidence. Data owner |
| Setting the index refresh | A freshness commitment with a threshold and an action on breach | Freshness monitoring specification. Operations owner |

**What this costs the organization.** A corpus with no accessions policy and no withdrawal policy becomes a second, uncontrolled system of record still answering from superseded documents. The cost people forget is re-embedding: changing the embedding model reprocesses everything, which is a budget event and a migration project rather than a configuration change.

**The executive translation.** We are creating a second copy of regulated records, so it needs an owner, a retention schedule and inherited access rules before it answers a single question.

---

## 5.4 Retrieval-augmented generation as a system

Retrieval-augmented generation is presented as a technique and operated as a system. **Thirteen stages across five owners, each stage with a distinct failure mode and a distinct instrument.** The seven design stages in 5.3 are the build-time view of this same system; in operation they expand into the thirteen stages below by two moves. Four stages that live outside the design session are added, source, parse, enrich and evaluate, and two of the design stages are split into their operating halves, embed from index and assemble from generate, because each half has a different owner and a different instrument. An architect who cannot name the stage that produced a bad answer cannot fix it, and will default to blaming the model, which is where most remediation budget is wasted.

```
  SOURCE  ->  INGEST ->  PARSE  -> ENRICH -> CHUNK -> EMBED
  (biz)      (data)     (data)    (data)   (arch)  (arch)
     |                                                 |
     +-----------------------------------------------+ |
                                                       v
  EVALUATE <- CITE <- GENERATE <- ASSEMBLE <- RERANK <- INDEX
   (quality) (arch)   (arch)      (arch)     (arch)  (platform)
     ^                                                 |
     |            RETRIEVE (arch) <--------------------+
     +---------------- query log ----------------------+
```

| Stage | Owner | What can go wrong here | The instrument that sees it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Source** | Business function | Wrong authority, stale content, missing content | The estate inventory |
| **Ingest** | Data engineering | Documents silently not collected; connector auth expiry | Document count reconciliation |
| **Parse** | Data engineering | Tables flattened, headers lost, scanned pages skipped, footnotes merged | Parse fidelity sampling |
| **Enrich** | Data engineering | Metadata missing, dates absent, access labels not propagated | Metadata completeness rate |
| **Chunk** | Architecture | Mid-idea cuts, orphan chunks, tables split across chunks | Manual chunk inspection |
| **Embed** | Architecture | Model mismatch to domain, silent dimension or version change | Embedding version log |
| **Index** | Platform | Staleness, partial rebuild, deleted content still present | Index freshness monitor |
| **Retrieve** | Architecture | Wrong k, filters not applied, permission filter after ranking | Recall at k on a labeled set |
| **Rerank** | Architecture | Correct chunk retrieved and reranked below the cut | Recall at k before and after rerank |
| **Assemble** | Architecture | Context truncation dropping the answer, ordering effects | Assembled-context capture |
| **Generate** | Architecture | Correct context, wrong reading. The genuine model failure | Faithfulness grading |
| **Cite** | Architecture | Citation points to a chunk that does not support the claim | Citation accuracy grading |
| **Evaluate** | Quality | Nothing measured, so nothing above is visible | The eval suite itself |

**⧉ The single largest risk in the whole chapter is failure attribution.** "The answer was wrong" is reported as a model defect roughly always and is a model defect roughly never. The distribution in practice is heavily weighted toward source, parse, enrich and retrieve. The consequence of misattribution is specific and expensive: teams upgrade models, rewrite prompts and add reasoning steps against a corpus problem, observe no improvement, conclude the technology is immature and stop. **An architect's most valuable single capability in a retrieval program is localizing a failure to one of thirteen stages within an hour.**

### The diagnostic table

| Symptom | Most likely stage | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confident answer contradicting the system of record | Source. Embedded knowledge indexed as text | Route to a tool call |
| Two users get two different answers to the same question | Source. Contradiction failure in the estate | Designate authority, deprecate the rest |
| Answer is generic and hedged, no citation to anything specific | Source. Absence failure | Commission the content |
| Whole document types never appear in results | Ingest or parse. Connector scope or unsupported format | Reconcile document counts against the source |
| Numbers wrong, surrounding text right | Parse. Table flattened into prose | Table-aware parsing; re-ingest the affected class |
| Answers ignore date or jurisdiction qualifiers | Enrich. Metadata absent, or present and not filtered on | Populate front matter; filter before ranking |
| Retrieved chunk is coherent but answers a different question | Chunk. Semantic drift within an oversized chunk | Re-chunk on structure |
| Quality dropped across the board with no code change | Embed or index. Model version change or partial rebuild | Compare embedding version; force a full rebuild |
| Right document exists, never returned | Retrieve. Query pattern mismatched to the index | Add lexical retrieval; check filters run before ranking |
| Right chunk returned at rank 15, cut at 5 | Rerank absent or misconfigured | Add reranking; measure recall before and after |
| Answer correct in short questions, wrong in long ones | Assemble. Truncation dropping the answer chunk | Budget the context; order by relevance |
| Context contains the answer, output does not use it | Generate. The real model failure | Prompt, model or effort change |
| Answer correct, citation does not support it | Cite. Attribution lost through assembly | Preserve chunk identity end to end |
| Correct at launch, wrong six months later | Index freshness plus corpus drift | Continuous labeled retrieval evaluation |

**Decision rule:** reproduce the failure with the retrieved chunks captured, and if the answer is wrong while the chunks are right, it is a generation failure; in every other case it is upstream of the model.

### Freshness, deletion, permission, tenancy and citation

**Five operational properties that are designed once and audited forever.**

**Freshness.** Every knowledge domain gets a stated **freshness requirement** expressed in time, not in effort: this domain must reflect source changes within four hours, that one within thirty days. Reindexing strategy follows from the requirement. Continuous incremental indexing for the hours-class, scheduled full rebuild for the months-class. **Publish the freshness commitment in the assistant's own interface**, because a user who knows the corpus is a day old reads a stale answer as a known limitation rather than as a lie.

**Deletion propagation.** When a document is deleted or superseded at source, it must disappear from every derived artifact: chunks, embeddings, index entries, caches, assembled-context logs and evaluation sets. **A deletion that reaches only the source is not a deletion.** ⚠ Where the deletion originates in a data subject erasure request or a legal hold release, the completeness of propagation is a regulatory matter and the derived-artifact map should be reviewed by counsel before the first request arrives, not after.

**Permission-aware retrieval.** The rule is single and absolute: **filter before you rank, never after.** Post-filtering leaks through result counts, latency, ranking behavior and, in citation-bearing systems, through the citations themselves. The user's own identity, not a service account, determines what is retrievable, which means the access labels captured at enrich must survive to query time. A system where the retrieval service has broad access and the application filters the output is one prompt injection away from a disclosure incident. **That is the confused deputy of 3.5, in retrieval form**: a privileged component acting on a request it cannot authorize, and 3.11 states the same ordering as an absolute at the database layer. The three sites are one rule, and none of the three is a compensating control for a broad-access retrieval service.

**Multi-tenant separation.** Three levels, and the choice is a risk decision rather than a cost decision:

| Level | Mechanism | When it is sufficient |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Logical** | Tenant identifier as a mandatory pre-filter | Internal tenants, low consequence of cross-contamination |
| **Namespace** | Separate index or collection per tenant | The common commercial default |
| **Physical** | Separate infrastructure per tenant | Regulated tenants, contractual isolation commitments |

**Decision rule:** if a single misconfigured filter could expose one tenant's content to another and that exposure would be notifiable, logical separation is insufficient.

**Citation and grounding.** Two distinct requirements. **Grounding** means the claim is supported by retrieved content. **Citation** means the system points at the specific content that supports it. A system can be grounded and uncited. It can be cited and ungrounded. It can fail both. Ungrounded-and-cited is the dangerous combination because it manufactures the appearance of evidence.

### The multilingual estate

**A multilingual corpus is the normal case in a global organization and nothing in a retrieval pipeline handles it by default.** An organization operating across the United States, the European Union and South Korea holds policy in one language, applies it in functions that work in two others and files with regulators in whichever language the regulator requires. The estate is multilingual before anybody decides it should be. The pipeline built over it is monolingual by construction rather than by choice, because every default in it was set by someone testing in one language, and it reports no error when a second language arrives.

Four places language breaks the pipeline, and none of them announces itself:

| Where it breaks | What happens | How it presents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Embedding quality** | Embedding models are not equally strong in every language, so recall varies by language across a corpus that looks uniform | One overall recall figure, high for the majority language and materially lower for the rest, with no visible boundary between them |
| **Cross-language retrieval** | A query in one language must find a passage in another and the match never surfaces | Silence. The document exists, the user asked correctly and nothing comes back, which is indistinguishable from absence |
| **Chunking** | Rules tuned for one script or writing system behave differently in another. Token counts, sentence boundaries, word segmentation and punctuation conventions all move | Chunks that are the right size in the language they were tuned on and half an idea or three ideas elsewhere |
| **Evaluation** | A pooled score reports the weighted average of what are effectively several different systems | A number that is true of no individual language and is best where the evaluation set is largest |

The fourth conceals the other three. An evaluation set assembled from whatever queries were available is dominated by the majority language, so its number moves when the majority language moves and stays flat when a minority language fails completely.

Three design responses, each cheap at design time and expensive later.

**Language is a required metadata field on every chunk**, populated at enrich, detected where it is not declared and never left null. Nothing else here can be built without it, because every other response is a per-language predicate and a predicate needs a field. It also makes uneven recall visible for the first time, since recall can be reported by language only where language was recorded.

**A decision is recorded per language pair** about whether cross-language retrieval is supported, whether the query is translated into the corpus language first or whether the pair is out of scope and the system says so. Three answers, one recorded choice per pair, and the pairs are enumerable because the languages are. A design that leaves this implicit has chosen the first option by accident and has not measured it.

**A separate evaluation set per language, with its own threshold**, rather than one pooled set with some multilingual cases in it. The pooled number is what conceals a language performing at half the rate of the rest, and it conceals it most effectively when the failing language serves the smallest population, which is frequently where the regulatory exposure sits. 8.2 states the general form of this requirement: report the correct rate by class rather than in aggregate, because an overall accuracy figure hides total failure on a rare class. Language is that class.

**The governance consequence, stated plainly.** A quality claim made without a per-language breakdown is not a claim about the languages the organization actually operates in. It is a claim about the majority language with the others averaged into it. Anyone asked to attest that an assistant performs at a stated level across a region should read the segment breakdown before signing, and where there is no breakdown, that is the finding.

**The translation question is separate and it is a legal one.** ⚠ Where a document exists in several languages, which version is authoritative is a question about the document rather than about the pipeline. A contract may name a governing language, a regulator may recognize only a filing in its own, and an internal policy may have been approved in one language and rendered into others for convenience. **An assistant citing a translation of a policy is citing something that may not be the policy.** The architectural requirements hold whichever way the legal question resolves: language and authoritative status are separate metadata fields, a translation is indexed as a translation rather than as the source, and the citation resolves to the authoritative version with the translation offered as a convenience. Which version governs, and whether an answer given from a translation carries the same weight as one given from the authoritative text, is a determination for counsel in each jurisdiction.

### Evaluating retrieval separately from generation

**Retrieval and generation must be measured with separate instruments against separate sets, because a good answer from bad retrieval and a bad answer from good retrieval are different defects with different owners.**

| Measure | What it asks | Set required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Recall at k** | Was the correct chunk in the top k? | Labeled query-to-chunk set |
| **Precision at k** | What fraction of the top k was relevant? | Same |
| **Mean reciprocal rank** | How high did the first correct chunk land? | Same |
| **Groundedness** | Is every claim in the answer supported by the provided context? | Answer-level grading |
| **Answer faithfulness** | Does the answer avoid asserting anything the context does not? | Answer-level grading |
| **Citation accuracy** | Does each citation actually support the sentence it is attached to? | Sentence-level grading |
| **Answer correctness** | Is the answer right, independent of the pipeline? | Golden question-answer set |

The pairing that localizes a failure: **high recall with low faithfulness is a generation problem; low recall with high faithfulness is a retrieval problem and the model is behaving correctly by declining to answer.** The second pattern is frequently misread as the model being unhelpful, and the remediation applied is a prompt change instructing it to try harder, which converts an honest abstention into a fabrication.

**Decision rule:** never report a single accuracy number for a retrieval system, because one number cannot distinguish the corpus failing, the retriever failing and the model failing.

---

## 5.5 The asset types

Enterprises use eleven names for written knowledge and use most of them interchangeably. They are not interchangeable, and an AI system consuming them behaves differently for each. **Precision here is not pedantry: it determines what the system is allowed to do with the content.**

| Asset | What it is for | Authored by | Approved by | Revision trigger | Behavior when an AI consumes it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Policy** | States what the organization requires or prohibits. Mandatory | Policy owner, legal | Executive or board committee | Regulatory change, incident, cycle review | Constraint. Should bound behavior, never be paraphrased loosely. Cite verbatim |
| **Standard** | States the mandatory how, at a measurable level | Function owner | Governance body | Technology or control change | Constraint with test conditions. Good source for automated checks |
| **Guideline** | Recommends. Not mandatory | Practitioner group | Function head | Practice evolution | Advisory. Must be labeled as such or the model presents preference as requirement |
| **Standard operating procedure** | The end-to-end way a recurring process is performed | Process owner | Function head, quality | Process change, audit finding | Executable sequence. The best raw material for agent workflows |
| **Work instruction** | Task-level steps for one role at one step | Team lead | Process owner | Tooling or role change | Narrow and highly executable. Frequently the most current document in the estate |
| **Runbook** | What to do when a specific named thing happens or breaks | Operations engineer | Operations lead | Incident, post-incident review | Conditional executable. Triggered, not browsed |
| **Playbook** | How to handle a situation class where judgment is required | Practice lead, legal | Function head | Precedent, regulatory change | Decision structure. Bounds the model's judgment rather than replacing it |
| **Template** | A reusable output shape | Practice lead | Function head, legal | Format or clause change | Output contract. Best supplied as structure, not as prose to imitate |
| **Checklist** | Verification that required items were done | Process owner | Quality, compliance | Failure, audit finding | Verification pass. Excellent as a post-generation grader |
| **Decision tree** | Deterministic routing across a finite condition set | Process owner | Function head, legal | Rule change | **Should not be retrieved.** Encode as code or a tool. A tree in prose gets read approximately |
| **Knowledge article** | An answer to a recurring question | Support or subject expert | Knowledge manager | Query gap, correction | General retrieval unit. Highest volume, lowest governance, fastest decay |

Three observations a review will reward. **A decision tree in a document is a deterministic rule that migrated into a model-owned step**, and it should be lifted into code with a test rather than indexed. **Guidelines mislabeled as policy are the most common source of over-refusal in enterprise assistants**, because the model treats a recommendation as a prohibition and declines valid work. And **knowledge articles decay fastest and are governed least**, which is the exact inversion of what a healthy estate looks like.

**Decision rule:** if the content is mandatory, cite it verbatim; if it is deterministic, execute it as code; if it is advisory, label it advisory in the retrieved text itself.

**This table cuts the same material as 1.7's five asset types and cuts it on a different axis.** 1.7 asks what belongs in a reuse library and how it is owned, versioned and promoted; this table asks how each type behaves when a model consumes it. The four that appear in both, playbook, runbook, template and standard operating procedure, carry the same definition in each. The **Approved by** column above is this section's governance artifact and it is why the section carries no separate lens block: the approval authority is already stated per row.

---

## 5.6 Playbooks and runbooks

A **playbook** handles a situation class where the right action depends on facts that vary and judgment is required. A **runbook** handles a specific named condition where the right action is known. **The distinction is whether the correct next step can be determined in advance.** Runbooks are triggered by a signal and executed; playbooks are entered by a human or an agent facing an open situation and worked.

Both must be written for two readers at once: an agent that will execute them and an auditor who will ask, months later, why a particular action was taken. That dual requirement produces a fixed structure.

### The seven required parts of an executable playbook

| Part | Requirement | What breaks without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Scope and trigger** | The situation class, stated as observable conditions | The playbook is applied to situations it was not written for |
| **Preconditions** | What must be true and verified before step one | Execution begins on missing or unverified facts |
| **Steps with owners** | Each step assigned to the agent, a system or a named human role | Silent over-assignment to the model |
| **Decision points** | Explicit branch conditions with the evidence each requires | The model invents a branch and it looks reasonable |
| **Escalation triggers** | Named conditions that stop execution and route to a human, with the destination | The unbounded run. The single most repeated failure in agent designs |
| **Evidence to capture** | What is recorded at each step, in what form, to what store | The action is unauditable, which for regulated work is the same as not having done it |
| **Exit criteria** | What completion looks like, and what an unsuccessful exit looks like | The agent cannot tell whether it is finished |

**Decision rule:** a playbook without escalation triggers and exit criteria is a description, not a procedure, and must not be given to an agent.

### Worked example: a data subject access request playbook in machine-consumable form

⚠ The response deadlines, verification standards and refusal grounds below are jurisdiction-specific and change; the structure is the transferable part and the specific values require confirmation with counsel for each jurisdiction the organization operates in.

```yaml
playbook_id: dsar-intake-and-fulfillment
owner: Data Protection Officer
approver: General Counsel
status: authoritative
effective_from: 2026-03-01
review_due: 2026-09-01
jurisdictions: [UK, EU]

scope:
  situation: An identifiable individual requests a copy of
    personal data the organization holds about them.
  applies_to: [privacy-ops, customer-service, legal]
  excludes:
    - Requests from law enforcement (see playbook le-disclosure)
    - Requests for correction or erasure (separate playbooks)

preconditions:
  - id: pre-1
    check: Request is from the data subject or a verified agent
    evidence: identity_verification_record
    on_fail: escalate.identity_unverified
  - id: pre-2
    check: Statutory response clock start date recorded
    evidence: clock_start_timestamp
    on_fail: halt

steps:
  - id: s1
    action: Classify request scope
    owner: agent
    output: {categories: [], date_range: {}, systems: []}
    evidence: scope_classification_record
  - id: s2
    action: Identify holding systems from the data map
    owner: agent
    tool: data_map_lookup
    note: Do not infer holdings from documentation. Query the
      data map. Systems not in the map are escalated, not
      assumed empty.
    evidence: data_map_query_record
    on_gap: escalate.unmapped_system
  - id: s3
    action: Retrieve records from each identified system
    owner: system
    evidence: retrieval_manifest_per_system
  - id: s4
    action: Apply exemption review
    owner: human
    role: privacy-counsel
    rationale: Exemption application is a legal judgment and is
      never assigned to the agent.
    evidence: exemption_decision_log
  - id: s5
    action: Compile and dispatch the response package
    owner: agent
    review: human
    role: privacy-ops
    evidence: [final_response_package, dispatch_timestamp]
    on_fail: halt

decision_points:
  - id: d1
    at: s4
    question: Does the response contain third-party personal
      data?
    branches:
      - condition: "no"
        goto: s5
      - condition: "yes, third party has consented"
        goto: s5
        evidence: third_party_consent_record
      - condition: "yes, no consent"
        goto: escalate.third_party_redaction
  - id: d2
    at: s1
    question: Is the request manifestly unfounded or excessive?
    branches:
      - condition: "no"
        goto: s2
      - condition: "uncertain or yes"
        goto: escalate.refusal_assessment
        note: Refusal is never an agent decision.

escalations:
  identity_unverified:
    to: privacy-ops queue
    sla_hours: 24
  unmapped_system:
    to: Data Protection Officer
    sla_hours: 8
    severity: high
  third_party_redaction:
    to: privacy-counsel
    sla_hours: 48
  refusal_assessment:
    to: privacy-counsel
    sla_hours: 24
    note: Regulatory exposure. Legal judgment required.

evidence_pack:
  required:
    - identity_verification_record
    - clock_start_timestamp
    - scope_classification_record
    - data_map_query_record
    - retrieval_manifest_per_system
    - exemption_decision_log
    - final_response_package
    - dispatch_timestamp
  retention: per records schedule RS-14
  store: case_management_system

exit_criteria:
  success:
    - Response dispatched before the statutory deadline
    - Every required evidence item present
    - Every exemption applied has a logged human decision
  unsuccessful:
    - "Deadline at risk: escalate to Data Protection Officer at
      60 percent of elapsed statutory period"
    - "Any required evidence item missing at dispatch: block
      dispatch"
```

Four properties make this machine-consumable rather than merely tidy. **Every step names its owner explicitly**, so over-assignment to the agent is visible on the page. **Every judgment step is assigned to a human by design and says why**, which is the difference between a control and an accident. **Every escalation names a destination and a time bound**, so escalation is a route rather than a stop. And **the evidence pack is enumerated**, which means completeness is checkable by code at exit rather than discovered at audit.

The same structure applies to a runbook with two changes: the trigger is a signal rather than a situation, and the decision points are conditions on system state rather than on judgment.

---

## 5.7 AI-searchable knowledge systems

The knowledge layer is architecture, not a folder. **Six components, each with an owner.**

```
  [ AUTHORITATIVE SOURCE REGISTRY ]   one row per domain,
        |    one owner, one authority
        v
  [ INGESTION CONTRACT ]   format, cadence, metadata,
        |    freshness, access labels, breach behavior
        v
  [ STAGING ]  parse -> enrich -> validate -> chunk preview
        |            |
        |            +-- fails validation -> back to owner
        v
  [ GOLDEN CORPUS ]  published, owned, dated, in force
        |                      ^
        |                      |
        v                      |
  [ SERVING INDEX ] --------> [ QUERY LOG ]
        |                      |
        v                      v
  [ DEPRECATION ]        [ COVERAGE BACKLOG ]
   tombstone, not delete   the highest-value list
                           in the enterprise
```

**The diagram shows eight boxes because it shows the six components plus the two artifacts they produce**, the serving index that the golden corpus feeds and the coverage backlog that the query log generates. The six components are the registry, the ingestion contracts, staging and publication, the golden corpus, deprecation and the query log, and each is named with its owner below.

**The authoritative source registry**, owned by knowledge governance, is one row per knowledge domain naming the single system or document that is authoritative, the human owner and the freshness requirement. It is the artifact that converts the estate inventory into a running control. Nothing enters the corpus that is not registered.

**Ingestion contracts** are agreements with each source system, not code, and they are owned by data engineering jointly with the named owner of the source system, because a contract one side can rewrite alone is not a contract. Each states the format supplied, the cadence, the metadata fields guaranteed, the access labels supplied, the freshness commitment and what happens when the contract is breached. **The breach clause is the part that matters**, because connectors fail silently and a source that stops delivering looks identical to a source with nothing new to say. The contract makes silence a detectable condition.

**The golden corpus** is the published, governed subset that the assistant is permitted to answer from. It is deliberately smaller than the estate. **Membership is a decision, not a default**, the decision belongs to knowledge governance, and it has three criteria: the content is authoritative, it has a living owner and it passes the orphan chunk test at section level.

**Staging and publication**, operated by data engineering, is a flow with a validation gate: parse, enrich, validate, preview the chunks, publish. Validation is automated and blocking, checking metadata completeness, effective dates present and not in the past, access labels present, parse fidelity above threshold and no orphan sections above a set proportion. **A document that fails validation goes back to its owner rather than into the index with a warning**, because warnings are not read.

**Deprecation and tombstoning**, called by the domain owner rather than by the platform. When content is superseded, it is not deleted from the knowledge system. It is **tombstoned**: removed from the serving index, retained in the archive and replaced by a record stating what superseded it and when. This matters for three reasons. Historic questions about what the rule was on a past date remain answerable. Citations in past outputs remain resolvable, which is an audit requirement. And a user who searches for the old document finds the tombstone rather than nothing, which is how they learn the rule changed.

**The query log as a knowledge management instrument**, read by the business function, which also owns the coverage backlog it produces. This is the most under-used asset in enterprise artificial intelligence. Every question the corpus could not answer is a costed, evidenced, demand-ranked request for content. **The list of questions your corpus cannot answer, ordered by frequency, is the highest-value backlog in the enterprise**, and it is generated for free by the system you already built. It routinely reveals that the most common question in a function has no written answer anywhere, which was true before the assistant existed and was invisible because people asked a colleague.

Four query-log categories, each routing differently:

| Category | Signal | Routes to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Answered and correct** | Positive feedback, no override | Nothing. Sample for evaluation |
| **Answered and wrong** | Override, correction, complaint | Failure attribution across the thirteen stages |
| **Not answered, content exists** | Low retrieval score, correct document present | Retrieval or document engineering |
| **Not answered, no content** | Low score, hand-search confirms absence | **The content backlog.** Route to the business owner |

**Knowledge coverage as a measured quantity.** Coverage is not "we indexed the wiki". Define it as the proportion of real query volume for which the golden corpus contains a correct, current, authoritative answer, measured by sampling the query log and hand-checking. Track it per domain. **A coverage number per domain converts an unbounded content program into a managed one**, and it is the number to show an executive sponsor because it explains the assistant's usefulness in one figure they can act on.

**Decision rule:** publish nothing into the golden corpus that lacks a registered authoritative source, a living owner and a passing validation run, and measure coverage per domain rather than per repository.

---

## 5.8 Knowledge governance

Five obligations. **Governance is what keeps a corpus correct after the people who built it move on**: its absence is why systems accurate at launch are wrong within a year with no code change.

| Obligation | The rule | The artifact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ownership** | Every retrievable document has a named living human owner with authority to change it | Ownership register, reconciled against the identity directory monthly |
| **Review cadence** | Every document has a review interval set by volatility and stakes, not by a uniform default | Review calendar with named reviewers |
| **Expiry** | Every document has a review-due date. Past due, it is flagged in retrieval; well past due, it is removed from the serving index | Expiry monitor |
| **Conflict resolution** | When two documents in one domain disagree, the registry's authority designation decides, and the loser is deprecated or scoped | Conflict log with resolution and date |
| **Retrievability** | **An unowned document must not be retrievable** | Enforced at publication, audited at index |

**The last rule is the one to state without hedging.** An unowned document cannot be corrected, reviewed, deprecated by anyone with standing or defended: serving it is not a governance shortfall but an unbounded liability with a citation attached. When ownership lapses, because nobody inherits it, the document leaves the serving index automatically: uncomfortable in month one, and the only mechanism that has kept a corpus healthy in year three, because ownership becomes a live obligation rather than an onboarding field.

**Conflict resolution needs a standing rule, not a case-by-case debate.** The default hierarchy: system of record beats document, authoritative beats derived, later effective date beats earlier, specific jurisdiction beats general. Where it does not resolve, the domain owner decides and logs it. ⚠ Where conflicting sources carry different regulatory weight, say a published regulatory expectation against an internal interpretation, the resolution is legal rather than knowledge management.

**Decision rule:** ownership lapse removes a document from the serving index automatically, because a document nobody will defend is one nobody should cite.

---

## Knowledge Architecture: the one-page version

1. The estate has three forms: explicit, tacit and embedded, and only explicit is a retrieval problem.
2. Three enterprise knowledge failures: absence, contradiction and invisibility, with three different owners.
3. Inventory on eight columns, and the authority column is the finding.
4. Document engineering has seven properties and one mechanical check, the orphan chunk test.
5. You cannot rewrite the corpus, so triage on query traffic against stakes and let the low-low quadrant leave the index.
6. Chunking is chosen by what the corpus is and indexing by how queries are phrased: two independent decisions over a three-by-three grid, merged by reciprocal rank fusion when the index is hybrid.
7. Ask first whether a corpus under roughly 200,000 tokens needs a pipeline at all.
8. Contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 plus reranking cut top-20 retrieval failure from 5.7 percent to 1.9 percent. The largest single reduction comes from contextual embeddings alone and the smallest from contextual BM25, which is nonetheless the step implementations skip.
9. Retrieval-augmented generation is thirteen stages across five owners, and the architect's core skill is localizing a failure to one of them, because wrong answers are usually a corpus or retrieval failure and are almost never a model failure.
10. Filter before you rank. Propagate deletion to every derived artifact. Measure retrieval and generation with separate instruments.
11. A multilingual estate breaks the pipeline in four places. Carry language as a required field on every chunk, record per language pair whether cross-language retrieval is supported or the query is translated first, and hold a separate evaluation set and threshold per language, because a pooled score is true of no language the organization operates in.
12. Eleven asset types behave differently under machine consumption, and a decision tree in prose belongs in code.
13. Playbooks need seven parts and are unsafe for an agent without escalation triggers and exit criteria.
14. The knowledge layer is a registry, ingestion contracts, staging, a golden corpus, tombstoned deprecation and a query log that produces the enterprise's best content backlog.
15. Governance is ownership, cadence, expiry, conflict rules and one absolute: **an unowned document must not be retrievable.**
